ai-at-work.title: Anthropic is operating a lab that conducts biology experiments
ai-at-work.excerpt: AI leaders have been promising that AI is the key to curing human disease. Anthropic researchers have also been warning that AI might kill us all.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic opened a biology lab to run actual experiments, putting their money where their mouth is on AI solving real problems like disease. This matters because every enterprise betting on AI-as-cure-all suddenly has a reference point for what responsible deployment actually looks like beyond the PowerPoint slides. Here's the thing though: if an AI safety company has to run their own lab to prove AI works in biology, what does that say about all the other vendors promising miracles without breaking a sweat or funding actual research?

ai-at-work.title: A new kind of AI model from a ChatGPT inventor is thrilling developers
ai-at-work.excerpt: Jev, a new kind of AI model, is showing developers a cheaper and faster path to software intelligence.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: OpenAI researchers have released Jev, a new AI model that promises to deliver software intelligence at a lower cost and faster speed than current options. For digital workplace teams building internal tools, chatbots, and automation features, this matters because it directly impacts your budget and deployment timelines when you're trying to actually ship something. Here's the reality though: cheaper and faster AI is great until you realize you're solving problems your users didn't ask you to solve in the first place.

ai-at-work.title: Disney’s first CTO led an AI startup it once accused of copying its characters
ai-at-work.excerpt: The former CEO of Character.AI, which Disney previously sent a cease-and-desist letter to, will serve as the company's first-ever chief technology officer.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Disney just hired a former CEO from Character.AI as its first CTO, which is the same company Disney once threatened with legal action for allegedly copying Disney characters. This matters because it shows how the entertainment industry's relationship with AI startups is shifting from adversarial to collaborative, and it suggests Disney sees real strategic value in understanding generative AI from the inside. The irony is almost too perfect: Disney went from "cease and desist" to "please come run our tech strategy," which either speaks to Character.AI's legitimacy or Disney's pragmatism, probably both.

ai-at-work.title: Data center builder Nscale files for IPO after multibillion-dollar Anthropic deal
ai-at-work.excerpt: Nscale Global Holdings Ltd. today filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange. The company, which builds data centers optimized for artificial intelligence workloads, didn’t reveal how much it h
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Nscale, a data center builder focused on AI infrastructure, just filed for an IPO after landing a massive deal with Anthropic and hitting a $14.6 billion valuation. This matters because digital workplace teams need to understand where the actual compute power behind their AI tools is coming from, and who's profiting from the infrastructure boom fueling enterprise AI adoption. Here's the thing though: everyone's racing to build data centers for AI while we still can't get our internal collaboration platforms to work properly without three separate vendors and a prayer.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft mops up after Patch Tuesday broke logins, audio, Excel
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft fixed hundreds of security flaws in its September Patch Tuesday software updates — but it also introduced some annoying bugs. Now it has fixed some of them with a series of out-of-band updat
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft's September Patch Tuesday updates fixed security holes but broke logins, audio, and Excel paste functions, forcing the company to release emergency hotfixes days later. This matters because broken core functionality after mandatory security patches puts IT teams in an impossible bind: apply patches and deal with user complaints, or delay patches and accept security risk. After three decades watching this cycle repeat, I can confidently say Microsoft's quality control has the consistency of a Windows update progress bar.

tools-tech.title: GhostCode attackers abuse device codes to take over Microsoft 365 accounts
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft 365 users are being tricked into handing over access to their accounts by a new phishing kit, GhostCode, that exploits a weakness in a legitimate device authorization flow. Researchers in eS
tools-tech.dwp_take: Attackers are using a phishing kit called GhostCode to trick Microsoft 365 users into giving up account access by exploiting the device code authentication flow that Microsoft designed to make login easier. This matters because device code flows are everywhere now, especially for headless applications and mobile scenarios, which means your users are increasingly exposed to this exact social engineering vector. The irony here is thick: Microsoft built this feature to improve security and user experience, and now it's become another way to get people to hand over the keys to the kingdom.

tools-tech.title: With Siri Recap, Apple threw a punch at OpenAI no one saw coming
tools-tech.excerpt: John Ternus’ Apple threw a curveball at OpenAI with Siri Recap on Apple Watch, accelerating a conversation about privacy and data protection in an AI-augmented digital era. It’s a move that may yet co
tools-tech.dwp_take: Apple launched Siri Recap on Apple Watch, a feature that summarizes your day using on-device AI rather than sending data to external servers like OpenAI's solutions do. For digital workplace folks, this matters because it signals that privacy-first AI processing is becoming table stakes, not a nice-to-have, which will reshape how we think about employee data and compliance. Honestly, watching Apple use privacy as a competitive weapon against OpenAI is the plot twist nobody expected, and it might finally force the industry to stop treating user data like it's just sitting there for the taking.

tools-tech.title: More and more people believe that AI will take away jobs rather than create new ones
tools-tech.excerpt: A new survey from the Pew Research Center shows that a majority of people worldwide now expect artificial intelligence to lead to fewer jobs rather than more. The survey is based on responses from 37
tools-tech.dwp_take: Most people surveyed across 37 countries believe AI will destroy jobs rather than create them, with wealthier nations most pessimistic about the outlook. Digital workplace leaders need to take this seriously because workforce anxiety directly impacts adoption, engagement, and the change management burden you're already carrying. Here's the thing: people aren't wrong to worry, but pretending everything will be fine while doing nothing to reskill your workforce is how you guarantee the bad outcomes everyone fears.

digital-culture.title: Thousands of security workers for Big Tech companies are on strike in California
digital-culture.excerpt: Security officers at some of the most prominent tech companies in Silicon Valley have been poised to walk off the job since voting to authorize a strike earlier this month. The workers have been in ta
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fourteen thousand security workers at major tech companies across Silicon Valley have voted to strike over stalled contract negotiations with security contractors. This matters because your digital workplace is only as secure as the people protecting it, and when those folks are underpaid and frustrated, your physical security posture starts crumbling. Here's the thing: tech companies spent billions on firewalls and AI security tools while the actual humans standing at the gates couldn't afford rent in the Bay Area. That's not a strategy, that's just asking for trouble.

digital-culture.title: Barclays workers in the U.K. demand extra pay to return to office
digital-culture.excerpt: Barclays workers in the United Kingdom are protesting the bank’s move from two office days a week to three (with senior staff expected four days) and demanding that the firm cover costs associated wit
digital-culture.dwp_take: Barclays UK employees signed an open letter demanding extra pay to offset the costs of increasing office days from two to three per week, with senior staff expected to be in four days starting October. This matters because it shows workers are finally doing the math on RTO costs and willing to push back collectively, which means companies can't just mandate office time without factoring in actual employee expenses. Here's the thing: Barclays probably thought three days was a reasonable compromise, but employees asking for hazard pay to commute is a sign they've stopped accepting RTO as a benign productivity play.

digital-culture.title: If the AI Industry Followed Its Own Research, It Might Have Paused Already
digital-culture.excerpt: Anthropic’s CEO says that safety hinges on understanding how AI “thinks.” So far the evidence is disturbing.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Anthropic's CEO admitted the AI industry doesn't actually understand how large language models work internally, yet keeps deploying them at scale anyway. This matters to digital workplace folks because you're about to inherit AI tools that your vendors can't fully explain, which makes governance, risk management, and trust conversations nearly impossible. Here's the thing: we spent decades building enterprise software with documented architecture and audit trails, and now we're supposed to confidently deploy black boxes that even their creators don't fully comprehend.

industry-news.title: Zuckerberg, Musk and Huang Reportedly Urged Trump to Reject AI Regulator
industry-news.excerpt: Zuckerberg, Musk, and Huang reportedly urged President Trump to reject an industry-funded AI regulator as debate over frontier AI oversight intensifies. The post Zuckerberg, Musk and Huang Reportedly
industry-news.dwp_take: Three tech billionaires lobbied Trump to block an industry-funded AI regulatory body, effectively pushing for lighter oversight of frontier AI development. This matters because workplace AI tools are rapidly becoming central to how we collaborate, communicate, and get work done, and the regulatory environment will directly shape what gets built and how safe it actually is. The irony here is thick: the same folks who've spent years saying they want "responsible AI" are apparently more interested in moving fast and breaking things, which is basically the startup motto that got us into most of the regulatory messes we have today.

industry-news.title: Samsung’s New Patent Reveals How a Galaxy Watch Could Measure Blood Sugar
industry-news.excerpt: A new Samsung patent reveals how wearable glucose measurement could work as the company continues researching noninvasive blood sugar monitoring. The post Samsung’s New Patent Reveals How a Galaxy Wat
industry-news.dwp_take: Samsung filed a patent for noninvasive blood sugar monitoring on a Galaxy Watch using wearable technology. For digital workplace professionals, this matters because employee wellness programs are moving from the break room to the wrist, and companies will soon be wrestling with data privacy questions they haven't even thought about yet. Here's the thing: just because we can measure someone's glucose on their smartwatch doesn't mean we should collect it all in an HR system, but I guarantee someone's already pitching that exact feature to their CHRO.

industry-news.title: AI Expansion, Robot Factories, and Escalating Security Threats Define This Week in Tech
industry-news.excerpt: See what you missed in Daily Tech Insider from Sept. 14–18. The post AI Expansion, Robot Factories, and Escalating Security Threats Define This Week in Tech appeared first on TechRepublic.
industry-news.dwp_take: AI is expanding across industries, robot factories are scaling up, and security threats are getting worse, according to TechRepublic's weekly roundup. Digital workplace pros need to care because these three trends are colliding directly over your infrastructure: smarter AI tools mean more data flying around, automated systems create new attack surfaces, and bad actors are getting better at exploiting both. Honestly, if your security team isn't already sweating through meetings about this convergence, they should be, because defending a workplace full of AI tools and connected robots is like securing a building where the locks keep learning new ways to open themselves.

industry-news.title: Vietnam Offers Businesses About $114K for AI Projects — Who Qualifies?
industry-news.excerpt: Vietnam's NATIF is offering businesses up to about $114,000 for AI projects, with applications open through Oct. 10, 2026. The post Vietnam Offers Businesses About $114K for AI Projects — Who Qualifie
industry-news.dwp_take: Vietnam's government is dangling $114K in subsidies for businesses willing to develop AI projects before October 2026. Digital workplace teams should care because this signals how seriously some governments are pushing AI adoption and funding innovation, which affects the global competitive landscape you're operating in. Look, free money for AI is great, but the real question is whether your organization actually has a legitimate AI problem to solve or if you're just chasing subsidies to build another chatbot nobody needs.
